Multiset Metric Dimension of Binomial Random Graphs

Austin Eide ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Toronto Metropolitan University, Toronto, ON, Canada; e-mail: austin.eide@torontomu.ca    Paweł Prałat ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Toronto Metropolitan University, Toronto, ON, Canada; e-mail: pralat@torontomu.ca
Abstract

For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and a subset R⊆VR\subseteq V, we say that RR is multiset resolving for GG if for every pair of vertices v,wv,w, the multisets {d⁡(v,r):r∈R}\{d(v,r):r\in R\} and {d⁡(w,r):r∈R}\{d(w,r):r\in R\} are distinct, where d⁡(x,y)d(x,y) is the graph distance between vertices xx and yy. The multiset metric dimension of GG is the size of a smallest set R⊆VR\subseteq V that is multiset resolving (or ∞\infty if no such set exists). This graph parameter was introduced by Simanjuntak, Siagian, and Vitrík in 2017 [19], and has since been studied for a variety of graph families. We prove bounds which hold with high probability for the multiset metric dimension of the binomial random graph 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) in the regime d=(n−1)​p=Θ⁡(nx)d=(n-1)p=\Theta(n^{x}) for fixed x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1).

1 Introduction

1.1 Background

For a finite, connected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and vertices v,w∈Vv,w\in V, we let d⁡(v,w)d(v,w) denote the distance between vv and ww, that is, the length of a shortest path in GG between vv and ww. For a vertex v∈Vv\in V and integer k≥0k\geq 0, we let

Sk​(v):={w∈V:d⁡(v,w)=k} and Nk​(v):={w∈V:d⁡(v,w)≤k}=⋃j=0kSj​(v)S_{k}(v):=\{w\in V\,:\,d(v,w)=k\}\quad\text{ and }\quad N_{k}(v):=\{w\in V\,:\,d(v,w)\leq k\}=\bigcup_{j=0}^{k}S_{j}(v)

be the sphere and, respectively, the ball of radius kk around vv. Similarly, for a subset V′⊆VV^{\prime}\subseteq V and k≥0k\geq 0, let

Sk​(V′):=⋃v∈V′Sk​(v) and Nk​(V′):=⋃v∈V′Nk​(v).S_{k}(V^{\prime}):=\bigcup_{v\in V^{\prime}}S_{k}(v)\quad\text{ and }\quad N_{k}(V^{\prime}):=\bigcup_{v\in V^{\prime}}N_{k}(v).

Finally, for V′,R⊆VV^{\prime},R\subseteq V, let

SkR​(V′):=Sk​(V′)∩R and NkR​(V′):=Nk​(V′)∩R.S_{k}^{R}(V^{\prime}):=S_{k}(V^{\prime})\cap R\quad\text{ and }\quad N_{k}^{R}(V^{\prime}):=N_{k}(V^{\prime})\cap R.

The metric signature of vv with respect to a set R⊆VR\subseteq V is the vector 𝒔R​(v):=(d⁡(v,w))w∈R∈ℕ0|R|\bm{s}_{R}(v):=(d(v,w))_{w\in R}\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{|R|}, where ℕ0{\mathbb{N}}_{0} is the set of non-negative integers. (We assume that the vertices of RR are ordered and that the indices of 𝒔R​(v)\bm{s}_{R}(v) are indexed with respect to this ordering.) We say that RR is metric resolving if 𝒔R​(v)≠𝒔R​(w)\bm{s}_{R}(v)\neq\bm{s}_{R}(w) for all v≠wv\neq w. The metric dimension of GG, denoted β⁡(G)\beta(G), is the size of a smallest metric resolving set for GG. Note that VV itself is always metric resolving, so β⁡(G)≤|V|\beta(G)\leq|V|. In fact, it is easy to see that for any connected graph GG, β⁡(G)≤|V⁡(G)|−1\beta(G)\leq|V(G)|-1 and the equality holds for G=KnG=K_{n}, the complete graph on nn vertices. We remark that the definition of a metric resolving set can be extended to cover graphs which are not connected by declaring that vertices in distinct components have distance ∞\infty; with this definition, the metric dimension of GG is simply the sum of the metric dimensions of its components.

The study of the metric dimension of graphs dates to the 1970s, when it was first proposed by Slater [20] and Harary and Melter [12]. Since then it has received significant attention from mathematicians and computer scientists, and the metric dimension is now known for a wide variety of graph families. We refer to the recent survey [21] for a fairly comprehensive list of these families, as well as some interesting applications. We make particular note of previous works on the metric dimension of random graphs. In [3], Bollobás, Mitsche, and Prałat investigated the metric dimension of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) when the average degree d=(n−1)​pd=(n-1)p is at least log5⁡n\log^{5}n; a recent paper of Díaz, Hartle, and Moore treats the cases log⁡n<d<log5⁡n\log n<d<\log^{5}n [5]. (Note that 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) is disconnected w.h.p.11 1 An event holds with high probability (w.h.p.) if it holds with probability tending to one as n→∞n\to\infty. for d≤(1−ϵ)​log⁡nd\leq(1-\epsilon)\log n, where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is an arbitrarily small constant.) Ódor and Thiran also consider a sequential version of metric dimension on 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) in which a player attempts to locate a hidden vertex v∗v^{*} by making sequential queries of the distances d⁡(v,v∗)d(v,v^{*}) for v∈Vv\in V [18, 17]. In [6], Dudek, English, Frieze, MacRury, and Prałat study a similar process on 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) in which the hidden vertex v∗v^{*} is allowed to move along an edge in each round. See also [7] for weaker bounds in the regime in which 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) has diameter two w.h.p. Lichev, Mitsche, and Prałat additionally study this process on random geometric graphs [15]. See also [16] for the metric dimension of random trees and very-sparse (d<1)(d<1) random graphs and [23] for related results on the stochastic block model.

Define the multiset signature of vv with respect to R⊆VR\subseteq V as the vector

𝒎R​(v):=(|SkR​(v)|)k=0diam​(G)∈ℕ0diam​(G)+1,\bm{m}_{R}(v):=(|S_{k}^{R}(v)|)_{k=0}^{\text{diam}(G)}\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{\text{diam}(G)+1},

where diam​(G)=maxu,v∈V⁡d⁡(u,v)\text{diam}(G)=\max_{u,v\in V}d(u,v) is the diameter of graph GG. Observe that 𝒎R​(v)\bm{m}_{R}(v) is a representation of 𝒔R​(v)\bm{s}_{R}(v) when 𝒔R​(v)\bm{s}_{R}(v) is considered as a multiset rather than a vector. A set RR is multiset resolving if 𝒎R​(v)≠𝒎R​(w)\bm{m}_{R}(v)\neq\bm{m}_{R}(w) for all v≠wv\neq w, and we define the multiset metric dimension βms​(G)\beta_{\text{ms}}(G) to be the size of a smallest multiset resolving set for GG if such a set exists, and define βms​(G)=∞\beta_{\text{ms}}(G)=\infty otherwise. This parameter was introduced by Simanjuntak, Siagian, and Vitrík in 2017 [19], and has since been studied by multiple authors—see, for instance, [1], [4], and [11]. As with metric resolving sets, the definition of a multiset resolving set can be extended to apply to graphs which are not connected.

A connected graph GG need not have finite multiset metric dimension; for instance, it is known that any non-path graph of diameter 22 has no multiset resolving set [19, Theorem 3.1]. To remediate this issue, Gil-Pons et. al. in [10] define the outer multiset metric dimension βmsout​(G)\beta_{\text{ms}}^{\text{out}}(G) as the size of a smallest RR such that 𝒎R​(v)≠𝒎R​(w)\bm{m}_{R}(v)\neq\bm{m}_{R}(w) for all v≠wv\neq w with v,w∈V∖R.v,w\in V\setminus R. Trivially, any set RR of size |V|−1|V|-1 is outer-multiset resolving, and hence always βmsout​(G)≤|V|−1\beta_{\text{ms}}^{\text{out}}(G)\leq|V|-1; in fact, it is shown in [14] that βmsout​(G)=|V|−1\beta_{\text{ms}}^{\text{out}}(G)=|V|-1 if and only if GG is regular and has diameter at most 22. Clearly we have βms​(G)≥βmsout​(G)\beta_{\text{ms}}(G)\geq\beta_{\text{ms}}^{\text{out}}(G) for any graph GG. On the other hand, we claim that βmsout​(G)≥β⁡(G)\beta_{\text{ms}}^{\text{out}}(G)\geq\beta(G). Indeed, if RR is outer-multiset resolving, then 𝒔R​(v)≠𝒔R​(w)\bm{s}_{R}(v)\neq\bm{s}_{R}(w) for all v≠wv\neq w with v,w∈V∖Rv,w\in V\setminus R; but it is easy to see that this is sufficient to ensure that 𝒔R​(v)≠𝒔R​(w)\bm{s}_{R}(v)\neq\bm{s}_{R}(w) for all v≠wv\neq w, so RR is also metric resolving. Hence,

βms​(G)≥βmsout​(G)≥β⁡(G).\beta_{\text{ms}}(G)\geq\beta_{\text{ms}}^{\text{out}}(G)\geq\beta(G).

Multiset resolving sets inherit some interesting applications from metric resolving sets. One example is source localization [21, Section 7.1]. Suppose that at time t=0t=0 a single (unknown) vertex v0v_{0} of a connected graph GG is infected, and that any uninfected vertex which is adjacent to an infected vertex at time t−1t-1 becomes infected at time tt, for each t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots. We would like to identify the source vertex v0v_{0} by observing the spread of the infection. One strategy for achieving this is to place a sensor at each vertex of some multiset resolving set RR for GG, with each sensor emitting a signal at the first moment its vertex becomes infected. For t=0,1,2,…t=0,1,2,\dots, let NtN_{t} be the number of signals emitted by vertices in RR at time tt. (Note that NtN_{t} is simply the number of vertices in RR at distance tt from v0v_{0}.) Then since RR is multiset-resolving for GG, the identity of v0v_{0} is completely determined by the sequence {Nt}t=0diam​(G)\{N_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\text{diam}(G)}.

Metric resolving sets have also been shown to be useful as a tool for certain instances of graph embedding, where the goal is map the vertices of GG to real NN-dimensional space while preserving structural properties of the graph. In applications, it is preferable for NN to be small. For example, in [22] the authors use small resolving sets to find low-dimensional embeddings of graphical representations of genomic sequences, allowing for the application of a variety of clustering algorithms. The embedding is obtained by mapping each vertex to its metric signature with respect to some small metric resolving set; thus, given a metric resolving set RR, the embedding maps the graph into ℝ|R|\mathbb{R}^{|R|}. Importantly, for the application considered in [22], the metric resolving set embedding is nearly an isometry, i.e., the Euclidean distance between the images of any pair of vertices is quite close to the graph distance between that pair.

Multiset signatures with respect to a multiset resolving set also provide a natural graph embedding, and we propose that this embedding could prove useful for some applications. While βms​(G)≥β⁡(G)\beta_{\text{ms}}(G)\geq\beta(G) for any graph GG, we observe that the dimension of the embedding produced by a multiset resolving set for GG has dimension diam​(G)+1\text{diam}(G)+1, as multiset signatures are vectors of this length. (Metric resolving set embeddings have dimension at least β⁡(G)\beta(G).) Our results demonstrate that for random graphs on nn vertices with average degree on the order of nxn^{x} for x>0x>0 sufficiently small, a multiset resolving set exists w.h.p.; since the diameter of this graph is O⁡(1x)O\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) w.h.p. (see [2]), we get an embedding into ℝO⁡(1x)\mathbb{R}^{O\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}. On the other hand, results from [3] show that corresponding metric resolving set embedding has dimension which is logarithmic in nn for the “best case” values of xx and polynomial in nn for the “worst case.” The extent to which either embedding preserves graph distances is an interesting question for future research.

1.2 Definitions

The binomial random graph 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) is formally defined as a distribution over the class of graphs with the set of vertices [n]:={1,…,n}[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\} in which every pair {i,j}∈([n]2)\{i,j\}\in\binom{[n]}{2} appears independently as an edge in GG with probability pp. Note that p=p⁡(n)p=p(n) may (and usually does) tend to zero as nn tends to infinity. Most results in this area are asymptotic by nature. For more about this model see, for example, [2, 9, 13].

We let d=(n−1)​pd=(n-1)p, where nn is the number of vertices and pp is the edge probability of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p). Given dd, we reserve the index i∗i^{*} to denote the largest integer i=i⁡(n)i=i(n) such that di=o⁡(n)d^{i}=o(n) as n→∞n\to\infty. We let c=c⁡(n)=di∗+1nc=c(n)=\frac{d^{i^{*}+1}}{n}. (These parameters essentially determine the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p).) To make our results simpler to state, we assume throughout that d=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)=Θ⁡(nx)d=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)}=\Theta(n^{x}) for some fixed x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), though we remark that the upper bound we obtain on βms​(𝒢​(n,p))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p)) can be extended to a more general setting. (See Section 5.) With this simplifying assumption on dd, we note that i∗=⌊1/x⌋i^{*}=\lfloor 1/x\rfloor, unless x=1/kx=1/k for some k≥2k\geq 2, in which case i∗=k−1i^{*}=k-1. In particular, i∗i^{*} is a function of xx alone (and not nn).

1.3 Concentration tools

Let X∈Bin​(n,p)X\in\textrm{Bin}(n,p) be a random variable distributed according to a Binomial distribution with parameters nn and pp. We will use the following consequences of Chernoff’s bound (see e.g. [13, Theorem 2.1]): for any t≥0t\geq 0 we have

Pr​(X≥E​X+t)\displaystyle\textsf{Pr}(X\geq\textsf{E}X+t) ≤\displaystyle\leq exp⁡(−t22​(E​X+t/3))\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2(\textsf{E}X+t/3)}\right) (1)
Pr​(X≤E​X−t)\displaystyle\textsf{Pr}(X\leq\textsf{E}X-t) ≤\displaystyle\leq exp⁡(−t22​E​X).\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\textsf{E}X}\right). (2)

Note that if t≤3​E​X2t\leq\frac{3\textsf{E}X}{2}, the right-hand side of (1) is at most exp⁡(−t23​E​X)\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{3\textsf{E}X}\right); since this also upper bounds (2), we have the following corollary: for any 0≤t≤3​E​X20\leq t\leq\frac{3\textsf{E}X}{2},

Pr​(|X−E​X|≥t)≤2​exp⁡(−t23​E​X).\textsf{Pr}(|X-\textsf{E}X|\geq t)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{3\textsf{E}X}\right). (3)

1.4 The function fx​(y)f_{x}(y)

For x∈(0,1]x\in(0,1], define the function fxf_{x} on [0,1][0,1] by

fx​(y):=∑i=0⌊1x⌋max⁡{i​x+y−1,0}.f_{x}(y):=\sum_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor}\max\{ix+y-1,0\}.

The function fxf_{x} arises naturally in the study of the lower and upper bounds for βms​(𝒢​(n,p))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p)), and we motivate its appearance in the context of each bound at the beginnings of their respective sections (Sections 3 and 4, respectively.) Here, we remark on some basic properties of fxf_{x}.

Lemma 1.1.

For x∈(0,1]x\in(0,1], the function fxf_{x} is continuous, identically 00 on [0,1−⌊1x⌋​x]\left[0,1-\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor x\right], and strictly increasing on [1−⌊1x⌋​x,1].\left[1-\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor x,1\right].

The proof of Lemma 1.1 is elementary and follows immediately from the definition of the function fx​(y)f_{x}(y), and so we omit it.

Lemma 1.2.

Let x∈(0,1]x\in(0,1] and y∈[0,1)y\in[0,1) be such that fx​(y)>0f_{x}(y)>0 (or, equivalently, that 1−⌊1x⌋​x<y<11-\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor x<y<1). Then for any ϵ∈[0,1−y]\epsilon\in[0,1-y], we have

fx​(y+ϵ)−fx​(y)≥ϵ.f_{x}(y+\epsilon)-f_{x}(y)\geq\epsilon.
Proof.

Since we assume that fx​(y)>0f_{x}(y)>0, it must be the case that the largest summand in fx​(y)f_{x}(y)—namely, max⁡{⌊1x⌋​x+y−1,0}\max\left\{\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor x+y-1,0\right\}—is positive. Increasing yy by ϵ\epsilon increases this summand by ϵ\epsilon; none of the other summands decrease after the change in yy, so the result follows. ∎

Lemma 1.3.

If x∈(0,1/8]x\in(0,1/8], then there is a unique solution y4=y4​(x)∈(0,1)y_{4}=y_{4}(x)\in(0,1) to fx​(y)=4.f_{x}(y)=4. Similarly, if x∈(0,1/2]x\in(0,1/2], then there is a unique solution y1=y1​(x)∈(0,1)y_{1}=y_{1}(x)\in(0,1) to fx​(y)=1.f_{x}(y)=1.

Proof.

We observe that, since the function fxf_{x} is continuous, identically 00 on [0,1−⌊1x⌋​x]\left[0,1-\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor x\right], and strictly increasing on [1−⌊1x⌋​x,1]\left[1-\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor x,1\right] by Lemma 1.1, as long as fx​(1)>4f_{x}(1)>4, there is necessarily a unique solution to fx​(y)=4f_{x}(y)=4 in (0,1)(0,1). We have

fx​(1)=∑i=0⌊1/x⌋i​x=(⌊1x⌋+1)​⌊1x⌋⋅x2.f_{x}(1)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor 1/x\rfloor}ix=\frac{\left(\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor+1\right)\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor\cdot x}{2}.

If x≤18x\leq\frac{1}{8}, then

(⌊1x⌋+1)​⌊1x⌋⋅x2>⌊1x⌋2≥82=4\frac{\left(\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor+1\right)\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor\cdot x}{2}>\frac{\left\lfloor\frac{1}{x}\right\rfloor}{2}\geq\frac{8}{2}=4

where we use (⌊1/x⌋+1)​x>1(\lfloor 1/x\rfloor+1)x>1 for x>0x>0.

The existence of a unique solution y1y_{1} to fx​(y)=1f_{x}(y)=1 for x∈(0,1/2]x\in(0,1/2] can be established using the same argument, since fx​(1)>1f_{x}(1)>1 for any x≤1/2x\leq 1/2. ∎

1.5 Main result

Our main result is the following.

Theorem 1.4.

If x∈(0,18]x\in\left(0,\frac{1}{8}\right] and d=(n−1)​p=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=(n-1)p=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)}, then w.h.p.

βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))≤ny4+O⁡(log−1⁡n),\beta_{\textup{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))\leq n^{y_{4}+O(\log^{-1}n)},

where y4=y4​(x)∈(0,1)y_{4}=y_{4}(x)\in(0,1) is the unique solution to fx​(y)=4f_{x}(y)=4. On the other hand, if x∈(0,12]x\in\left(0,\frac{1}{2}\right] and d=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)}, then w.h.p.

βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))≥ny1+O⁡(log−1⁡n),\beta_{\textup{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))\geq n^{y_{1}+O(\log^{-1}n)},

where y1=y1​(x)y_{1}=y_{1}(x) is the unique solution to fx​(y)=1f_{x}(y)=1. Finally, if x>12x>\frac{1}{2}, then w.h.p.

βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))=∞.\beta_{\textup{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))=\infty.

We remark that Theorem 1.4 is equivalent to saying that if d=Θ⁡(nx)d=\Theta(n^{x}) for some fixed x∈(0,1/8],x\in(0,1/8], then βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))=O⁡(ny4​(x))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))=O(n^{y_{4}(x)}) w.h.p., and if d=Θ⁡(nx)d=\Theta(n^{x}) for fixed x∈(0,1/2]x\in(0,1/2], then βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))=Ω⁡(ny1​(x))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))=\Omega(n^{y_{1}(x)}) w.h.p. (Recall from Lemma 1.3 that the equation fx​(y)=4f_{x}(y)=4 has a unique solution if x∈(0,1/8]x\in(0,1/8], and fx​(y)=1f_{x}(y)=1 has a unique solution if x∈(0,1/2].x\in(0,1/2].) The gap between the lower and upper bounds is still quite large; indeed, for the range of xx for which both bounds apply, the ratio of the upper bound to the lower goes to infinity polynomially in nn. It is also still uncertain whether βms​(𝒢​(n,p))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p)) is even finite w.h.p. for x∈(18,12]x\in\left(\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{2}\right]. The result for x>12x>\frac{1}{2} follows from the fact that βms​(G)=∞\beta_{\text{ms}}(G)=\infty for any non-path graph GG of diameter at most 22 [19, Theorem 3.1], and the fact that 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) has diameter 22 w.h.p. in the regime d=nxd=n^{x} for 12<x<1\frac{1}{2}<x<1 [2].

In Figure 1 we plot the functions y1​(x)y_{1}(x) and y4​(x)y_{4}(x). Each curve exhibits the type of “zig-zag” behaviour also observed for the metric dimension of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) in [2], with jumps occurring at reciprocals of integers 1k\frac{1}{k} for k≥1.k\geq 1. Note that these are precisely the points at which the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) decreases from k+1k+1 to kk. While obtaining a general formula for y1​(1/k)y_{1}(1/k) and y4​(1/k)y_{4}(1/k) appears difficult, with an ad hoc approach they are manageable to compute for specific values of kk. For instance, we found that y1​(1/2)=3/4y_{1}(1/2)=3/4, y1​(1/3)=2/3y_{1}(1/3)=2/3, y1​(1/4)=7/12y_{1}(1/4)=7/12, and so on.

2 Expansion properties

Here we outline some useful expansion properties of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) which hold w.h.p. in the regime we are interested in. We are particularly concerned with the sizes of the shells Si​(v)S_{i}(v) and Si​({u,v})S_{i}(\{u,v\}) for vertices uu, vv, and distances i≥0i\geq 0. Let d=(n−1)​pd=(n-1)p satisfy ω⁡(log⁡n)=d=o⁡(n)\omega(\log n)=d=o(n). Recall that we let i=i∗​(n)i=i^{*}(n) be the largest integer ii such that di=o⁡(n)d^{i}=o(n) and c=c⁡(n)=di∗+1n.c=c(n)=\frac{d^{i^{*}+1}}{n}. Define γ=max⁡{log⁡nd,di∗n}=o⁡(1)\gamma=\max\left\{\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}},\frac{d^{i^{*}}}{n}\right\}=o(1). For V′⊆VV^{\prime}\subseteq V and i∈{0,1,2,…,i∗}i\in\{0,1,2,\dots,i^{*}\}, define the events

𝒱i(V′)={|Si(V′)|=(1+O(γ))|V′|di}.\mathcal{V}_{i}(V^{\prime})=\left\{\,|S_{i}(V^{\prime})|=(1+O(\gamma))|V^{\prime}|d^{i}\,\right\}.

and

𝒱i∗+1(V′)={|Si(V′)|=(1−e−|V′|​c−|V′|​di∗n+O(γ+log⁡nn))n}.\mathcal{V}_{i^{*}+1}(V^{\prime})=\left\{\,|S_{i}(V^{\prime})|=\left(1-e^{-|V^{\prime}|c}-\frac{|V^{\prime}|d^{i^{*}}}{n}+O\left(\gamma+\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right)n\,\right\}.

Let

𝒱:=⋂V′:|V|′∈{1,2}⋂i=0i∗+1𝒱i(V′).\mathcal{V}:=\bigcap_{V^{\prime}:|V|^{\prime}\in\{1,2\}}\bigcap_{i=0}^{i^{*}+1}\mathcal{V}_{i}(V^{\prime}).

All of our results rely on the following lemma. We note that while our main results on the multiset metric dimension only apply to random graphs with average degree on the order of nxn^{x} for fixed x>0x>0, the lemma establishes typical expansion properties of random graphs down to degree d=ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\omega(\log n).

Lemma 2.1.

Suppose d=(n−1)​pd=(n-1)p satisfies d=ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\omega(\log n) and d=o⁡(n)d=o(n). Then the event 𝒱\mathcal{V} holds w.h.p. in 𝒢⁡(n,p).\mathcal{G}(n,p).

A version of Lemma 2.1 was originally shown to hold for (log⁡n)5​(log⁡log⁡n)2≤d=o⁡(n)(\log n)^{5}(\log\log n)^{2}\leq d=o(n) in [3]; it was subsequently shown in [18] to hold with the hypothesis ω⁡(log⁡n)=d=o⁡(n)\omega(\log n)=d=o(n). We refer the reader to those sources for the proof. In particular, for levels i=0,1,…,i∗i=0,1,\dots,i^{*} see [18, Lemma 5.1], and for level i=i∗+1i=i^{*}+1 see [18, Lemma 5.3] (a mild extension is required for the latter case). We summarize some useful consequences of Lemma 2.1 in the following corollary, which is easily deduced from the lemma.

Corollary 2.2.

Let d=(n−1)​pd=(n-1)p satisfy d=ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\omega(\log n) and d=o⁡(n)d=o(n). Then the following hold w.h.p. for 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p):

  1. (i)

    For any vertex vv and any i∈{0,1,…,i∗}i\in\{0,1,\dots,i^{*}\}, |Ni​(v)|=(1+o⁡(1))​di|N_{i}(v)|=(1+o(1))d^{i}.

  2. (ii)

    For any pair of vertices vv and ww and any i∈{0,1,…,i∗}i\in\{0,1,\dots,i^{*}\}, |Si​(w)∖Ni​(v)|=(1+o⁡(1))​di|S_{i}(w)\setminus N_{i}(v)|=(1+o(1))d^{i}.

  3. (iii)

    If c=Θ⁡(1)c=\Theta(1), for any vertex vv, |Ni∗+1​(v)|=(1+o⁡(1))​(1−e−c)​n|N_{i^{*}+1}(v)|=(1+o(1))(1-e^{-c})n.

  4. (iv)

    If c=Θ⁡(1)c=\Theta(1), for any pair of vertices vv and ww, |Si∗+1​(v)∖Ni∗​(w)|=(1+o⁡(1))​(1−e−c)​n|S_{i^{*}+1}(v)\setminus N_{i^{*}}(w)|=(1+o(1))(1-e^{-c})n and |Si∗+1​(w)∖Ni∗+1​(v)|=(1+o⁡(1))​e−c​(1−e−c)​n|S_{i^{*}+1}(w)\setminus N_{i^{*}+1}(v)|=(1+o(1))e^{-c}(1-e^{-c})n.

3 Upper bound

Throughout this section, we will condition on 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) having the typical expansion property 𝒱\mathcal{V}, so that in particular all statements in Corollary 2.2 hold. To prove the upper bound, we use a standard application of the probabilistic method. Our strategy is to show that a random subset of vertices RR chosen by including each vertex independently with probability r/nr/n has the following property when r=r⁡(n)r=r(n) is sufficiently large with respect to d=(n−1)​pd=(n-1)p: for any pair of vertices v,wv,w,

Pr​(R​ fails to distinguish ​v​ and ​w|𝒱)≤12​n2.\textsf{Pr}(R\text{ fails to distinguish }v\text{ and }w\,|\,\mathcal{V})\leq\frac{1}{2n^{2}}. (4)

Then by a union bound, the probability that RR fails to distinguish some pair is at most (n2)⋅12​n2≤14\binom{n}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2n^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{4}. By Markov’s inequality, the probability that RR is at least 2​E​[|R|]=2​r2\textsf{E}[|R|]=2r is at most 12\frac{1}{2}. Thus the probability that RR is a multiset resolving set and |R|≤2​r|R|\leq 2r is at least 14\frac{1}{4}, allowing us to conclude that 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) has a mutliset resolving set of size at most 2​r2r conditional on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. (In practice, rr will be o⁡(n)o(n), so the bound is nontrivial.) Since 𝒱\mathcal{V} holds w.h.p., we get βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))≤2​r\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))\leq 2r w.h.p.

In the proof, we show that if d=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)} for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), the bound (4) holds when the parameter rr is of the order nyn^{y}, where yy satisfies fx​(y)≥4f_{x}(y)\geq 4. A heuristic explanation is as follows. Recall that i∗i^{*} is the largest ii so that di=o⁡(n)d^{i}=o(n). Note first that if RR fails to distinguish vv and ww, then |SiR​(v)∖Si​(w)|=|SiR​(w)∖Si​(v)||S_{i}^{R}(v)\setminus S_{i}(w)|=|S_{i}^{R}(w)\setminus S_{i}(v)| for all ii, since each vertex in SiR​({v,w})S_{i}^{R}(\{v,w\}) contributes equally to |SiR​(v)||S_{i}^{R}(v)| and |SiR​(w)||S_{i}^{R}(w)|. For each i∈{0,1,…,i∗}i\in\{0,1,\dots,i^{*}\}, |SiR​(v)∖Si​(w)||S_{i}^{R}(v)\setminus S_{i}(w)| and |SiR​(w)∖Si​(v)||S_{i}^{R}(w)\setminus S_{i}(v)| are independent binomial random variables with means (1+o⁡(1))​μi(1+o(1))\mu_{i}, where we define μi=di​rn=Θ⁡(ni​x+y−1)\mu_{i}=\frac{d^{i}r}{n}=\Theta(n^{ix+y-1}) when r=nyr=n^{y}. We can then bound the probability that |SiR​(v)∖Si​(w)|=|SiR​(w)∖Si​(v)||S_{i}^{R}(v)\setminus S_{i}(w)|=|S_{i}^{R}(w)\setminus S_{i}(v)| by min{1,O(μi−1/2)}=O(n−12​max⁡{i​x+y−1,0})\min\{1,\,O(\mu_{i}^{-1/2})\}=O\left(n^{-\frac{1}{2}\max\{ix+y-1,0\}}\right). (This bound corresponds to the maximum of the probability mass function of the Bin​(di,r/n)\text{Bin}(d^{i},r/n) random variable, see Lemma 3.2.) If all of the variables |SiR​(v)∖Si​(w)||S_{i}^{R}(v)\setminus S_{i}(w)| and |SiR​(w)∖Si​(v)||S_{i}^{R}(w)\setminus S_{i}(v)| were independent for i∈{0,1,…,i∗}i\in\{0,1,\dots,i^{*}\}, we could bound the probability that RR fails to distinguish vv and ww by

O(∏i=0i∗n−12​max⁡{i​x+y−1,0})=n−12∑i=0i∗max{ix+y−1,0}+O(log−1n).O\left(\prod_{i=0}^{i^{*}}n^{-\frac{1}{2}\max\{ix+y-1,0\}}\right)=n^{-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=0}^{i^{*}}\max\{ix+y-1,0\}+O(\log^{-1}n)}. (5)

In the event, the independence assumption does not hold, since (Si​(v)∖Si​(w))∩(Sj​(w)∖Sj​(v))(S_{i}(v)\setminus S_{i}(w))\cap(S_{j}(w)\setminus S_{j}(v)) can be nonempty for i≠ji\neq j. Even so, by taking a bit more care in the proof we can show that a bound like (5) still holds. When 1k+1<x<1k\frac{1}{k+1}<x<\frac{1}{k} for some positive integer kk, we have i∗=k=⌊1/x⌋i^{*}=k=\lfloor 1/x\rfloor, and thus the righthand side of (5) is precisely n−12​fx​(y)+O⁡(log−1⁡n)n^{-\frac{1}{2}f_{x}(y)+O(\log^{-1}n)}, suggesting that yy must be large enough so that fx​(y)≥4f_{x}(y)\geq 4 in order for (4) to hold. An extension of this argument shows that the same situation holds when x=1kx=\frac{1}{k}. Lemma 1.3 gives that we may choose such a yy provided that 0<x≤1/80<x\leq 1/8.

The main result on the upper bound can now be properly stated.

Theorem 3.1.

Let x∈(0,18]x\in\left(0,\frac{1}{8}\right] be fixed and let d=(n−1)​p=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=(n-1)p=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)}. W.h.p., 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) has a multiset resolving set of size at most ny4+O⁡(log−1⁡n)n^{y_{4}+O(\log^{-1}n)}, where y4=y4​(x)∈(0,1)y_{4}=y_{4}(x)\in(0,1) is the unique solution to fx​(y)=4f_{x}(y)=4.

Lemma 3.2.

Let ZZ be a binomial random variable with mean μ\mu. Then

maxz⁡Pr​(Z=z)≤min⁡{1,O⁡(1μ)}.\max_{z}\textsf{Pr}(Z=z)\leq\min\left\{1,O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}\right)\right\}.

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 3.1.

4 Lower bound

To illustrate the proof of the lower bound, let x∈(1k+1,1k]x\in\left(\frac{1}{k+1},\frac{1}{k}\right] for some k≥2k\geq 2 and d=(n−1)​p=Θ⁡(nx)d=(n-1)p=\Theta(n^{x}). We will make use of the following result on the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) from [2]:

Lemma 4.1 ([2, Corollary 10.12]).

Let d=(n−1)​p=ω⁡(log⁡n)d=(n-1)p=\omega(\log n), and suppose

di−1n−2​log⁡n→−∞ and din−2​log⁡n→∞.\frac{d^{i-1}}{n}-2\log n\to-\infty\quad\text{ and }\quad\frac{d^{i}}{n}-2\log n\to\infty.

Then, the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) equals ii w.h.p.

For our choice of xx, by Lemma 4.1 the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) is k+1k+1 w.h.p. This means that for any set RR and any vertex vv, the multiset signature 𝒎R​(v)\bm{m}_{R}(v) of vv with respect to RR is w.h.p. fully determined by the first kk coordinates, i.e., by |SiR​(v)||S_{i}^{R}(v)| for i∈{0,1,…,k}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}. Using a simple counting argument, we will show that w.h.p. in 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p), for any set RR, at least (1+o⁡(1))​n2(1+o(1))\frac{n}{2} vertices have the property that |SiR​(v)|≤max⁡{1,O⁡(di​|R|n)}|S_{i}^{R}(v)|\leq\max\left\{1,O\left(\frac{d^{i}|R|}{n}\right)\right\} for all i∈{0,1,…,k}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}. For these typical vertices, when |R|≤ny|R|\leq n^{y}, the number of possible signatures with respect to RR is then crudely at most

∏i=0kmax⁡{1,O⁡(di​|R|n)}=O⁡(∏i=0knmax⁡{i​x+y−1,0})=nfx​(y)+O⁡(log−1⁡n).\prod_{i=0}^{k}\max\left\{1,O\left(\frac{d^{i}|R|}{n}\right)\right\}=O\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k}n^{\max\{ix+y-1,0\}}\right)=n^{f_{x}(y)+O(\log^{-1}n)}.

If the righthand side above is less than, say, 0.49​n0.49n, then we may conclude that there must be some pair of typical vertices v,wv,w with 𝒎R​(v)=𝒎R​(w)\bm{m}_{R}(v)=\bm{m}_{R}(w). Recall that by Lemma 1.3 there exists a solution y1=y1​(x)∈(0,1]y_{1}=y_{1}(x)\in(0,1] to the equation fx​(y)=1f_{x}(y)=1 when 0<x≤1/2.0<x\leq 1/2. Let y=y1−Clog⁡ny=y_{1}-\frac{C}{\log n} for a constant C>0C>0. By Lemma 1.2 we have fx​(y)≤fx​(y1)−Clog⁡n=1−Clog⁡nf_{x}(y)\leq f_{x}(y_{1})-\frac{C}{\log n}=1-\frac{C}{\log n}. Thus if CC is chosen sufficiently large, then nfx​(y)+O⁡(log−1⁡n)n^{f_{x}(y)+O(\log^{-1}n)} can be made less than 0.49​n0.49n, which yields the desired result.

Theorem 4.2.

Let x∈(0,12]x\in\left(0,\frac{1}{2}\right] be fixed and let d=(n−1)​p=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=(n-1)p=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)}. W.h.p., 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) has no multiset resolving set of size less than ny1+O⁡(log−1⁡n)n^{y_{1}+O(\log^{-1}n)}, where y1=y1​(x)∈(0,1)y_{1}=y_{1}(x)\in(0,1) is the unique solution to fx​(y)=1f_{x}(y)=1.

Note that the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) is 22 for x>12x>\frac{1}{2}, in which case there is no multiset resolving set for 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) by a result from [19].

Proof.

|AiR|≤n2​(k+1)⋅maxw∈AiR⁡|Ni​(w)|minv∈R⁡|Ni​(v)|=(1+o⁡(1))​n2​(k+1)|A_{i}^{R}|\leq\frac{n}{2(k+1)}\cdot\frac{\max_{w\in A_{i}^{R}}|N_{i}(w)|}{\min_{v\in R}|N_{i}(v)|}=(1+o(1))\frac{n}{2(k+1)}

where the last equality holds from the fact that |Ni​(w)|=(1+o⁡(1))​|Ni​(v)||N_{i}(w)|=(1+o(1))|N_{i}(v)| for all pairs vv and ww and all i∈{0,1,…,k}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\} by Corollary 2.2 (i). Now, since the diameter is k+1k+1, for any R⊆VR\subseteq V and v∈Vv\in V, the signature 𝒎R​(v)\bm{m}_{R}(v) is fully determined by the coordinates 0,1,…,k0,1,\dots,k. Thus, if vv is typical with respect to RR, then for any i∈{0,1,…,k}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}, there are at most

max⁡{(1+o⁡(1))​2​(k+1)​di​rn, 1}=O⁡(max⁡{ni​x+y−1,1})=O⁡(nmax⁡{i​x+y−1,0})\max\left\{(1+o(1))2(k+1)\frac{d^{i}r}{n},\,1\right\}=O\left(\max\{n^{ix+y-1},1\}\right)=O\left(n^{\max\{ix+y-1,0\}}\right) (7)

possibilities for the iith coordinate of 𝒎R​(v)\bm{m}_{R}(v). Therefore, the number of signatures which are allowed for typical vertices is at most

The argument above extends easily to the case that x=1kx=\frac{1}{k} for some positive integer k≥2k\geq 2. In this case we have i∗=k−1i^{*}=k-1, so the bound (7) holds for any i∈{0,1,…,k−1}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k-1\} in this case. possible signatures for typical vertices, and the rest of the argument follows as before. ∎

5 Conclusion

We have shown that for the regime d=(n−1)​p=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=(n-1)p=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)} for fixed 0<x≤1/80<x\leq 1/8, the muiltiset metric dimension βms​(𝒢​(n,p))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p)) of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) satisfies βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))≤ny4+O⁡(log−1⁡n)\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))\leq n^{y_{4}+O(\log^{-1}n)} w.h.p., and for fixed 0<x≤120<x\leq\frac{1}{2}, βms​(𝒢⁡(n,p))≥ny1+O⁡(log−1⁡n)\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p))\geq n^{y_{1}+O(\log^{-1}n)} w.h.p., where y4y_{4} and y1y_{1} are constants in (0,1)(0,1) which are explicitly computable from xx. We chose the scaling d=nx+O⁡(log−1⁡n)d=n^{x+O(\log^{-1}n)} primarily to make our results cleaner to state. However, the upper bound can be extended to the more general setting d=ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\omega(\log n); indeed our argument depends only on 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) satisfying the typical expansion profile guaranteed by Lemma 2.1, which holds w.h.p. for d=ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\omega(\log n). In principle, the lower bound can also be extended to this regime, though the arguments there also depend on knowing the diameter of 𝒢⁡(n,p)\mathcal{G}(n,p) w.h.p.

We propose two directions for future research. The first is to determine whether βms​(𝒢​(n,p))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p)) is finite w.h.p. for d=nxd=n^{x}, 18<x≤12\frac{1}{8}<x\leq\frac{1}{2}. The second is to tighten the gap between the lower and upper bounds for βms​(𝒢​(n,p))\beta_{\text{ms}}(\mathcal{G}(n,p)) for x∈(0,12)x\in(0,\frac{1}{2}). New proof strategies are likely needed for both problems.
